facebook.post: Picture this: a quiet evening in historic Longmont. A man sits in the parlor with his wife when a bullet suddenly crashes through the front window, killing him almost instantly. His son, Rienzi, was arrested on suspicion of inheritance-motivated murder — but he was never convicted. The case remains unsolved to this day, and the building at 303 Kaufman still stands downtown. We explore this dark chapter of local history in the latest episode of SideDish Longmont. Have you ever walked past that building and wondered about its past?

As one of our guests put it, leave it to a woman from New England to look at the Wild West and say, "you're gonna be learned." What other surprising pieces of early Longmont history do you know?

facebook.post: Hard to imagine now, but Longmont was once a dry town. If you wanted a drink, you had to walk six blocks north to the bars in what was technically North Longmont, a separate community. The catch? If police picked you up for drunkenness on your walk back down Main Street, you were now officially drunk in Longmont and could be arrested. It's wild to think about this history when Longmont is known today for its breweries and beer culture. What other quirky Longmont history have you heard?
